RRSP versus TFSA in four charts: compare the same after-tax saving effort

Follow the deduction, growth and withdrawal tax through a fair comparison. See why the tax-rate relationship matters when the saving budget is held constant.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore RRSP and TFSA tax timing

Interactive planning lab

RRSP gross contribution$16,666.67
RRSP after assumed tax$30,955.14
TFSA ending amount$26,532.98

Hypothetical one-time contribution comparison with the same net saving cost today. RRSP contribution is grossed up using fully usable immediate tax relief; sufficient contribution and deduction room is assumed. Both accounts earn the same constant effective annual return. RRSP balances are shown after an assumed full withdrawal at one constant tax rate. TFSA qualified growth and withdrawals are assumed tax-free. No benefit interactions, refund delay, fees, account limits or other tax rules are modeled.

The central idea

Compare the spendable outcome from the same net saving cost. A gross account balance alone does not show the money available after tax.

01

Begin with the different tax timing

The Canada Revenue Agency’s RRSP overview explains that deductible contributions can reduce tax, income inside the plan is usually sheltered while it remains there, and payments are generally taxable. The CRA’s TFSA overview explains that contributions are not deductible and qualifying account income and withdrawals are generally tax-free.

The charts isolate those mechanics. They assume both accounts hold investments earning exactly the same return and both have enough available room for the modeled contribution. They do not select investments, calculate eligibility or estimate an individual’s actual tax bill.

Tax relief and withdrawal tax are entered as constant percentages applying to the full relevant amount. Real deductions and withdrawals can span brackets and interact with other income, benefits and credits. The percentages here are hypothetical assumptions, not published federal or provincial tax rates.

02

Hold the personal saving cost constant

Suppose the available after-tax saving budget is B and the tax relief on a fully deductible RRSP contribution is t. The modeled gross RRSP contribution is B ÷ (1 − t). Tax relief finances the difference between that contribution and B. The TFSA receives B directly.

For a CAD 10,000 personal budget and 40% tax relief, the RRSP contribution is CAD 16,666.67. The assumed tax relief is CAD 6,666.67, leaving CAD 10,000 of net cost. The TFSA contribution is CAD 10,000. Comparing those gross deposits without their tax treatment would miss why they differ.

This assumes the relief is usable immediately and funds the larger deposit, such as through a suitably arranged cash-flow process. A refund received later creates a timing or financing issue. If the refund is spent rather than included in saving, that is a different comparison with different consumption today. The tool does not model a refund delay or borrowing costs.

03

Read the after-tax bars and the growth paths

The ending-balance chart displays account value and modeled spendable value. For the RRSP, the second bar deducts the assumed withdrawal tax from the entire balance. For the TFSA, the two bars coincide under the qualifying tax-free treatment assumed here.

With 20 years at 5%, the default TFSA reaches CAD 26,532.98. The grossed-up RRSP, after a hypothetical 30% tax on its full withdrawal, leaves CAD 30,955.14. The difference comes from the selected tax-rate relationship, with identical growth assumptions and net initial saving costs.

The line chart shows the same comparison at earlier dates. Each RRSP point assumes a complete withdrawal at that date using the same selected tax rate. It is not a sequence of annual withdrawals, an income drawdown strategy or a calculation of mandatory registered-account payments. The selected return is smooth and uncertain in practice.

04

Use the matrix to see the equal-rate result

If the RRSP deduction relief and withdrawal rate are equal, the model produces the same spendable outcome as the TFSA. Algebraically, RRSP net ÷ TFSA = (1 − withdrawal rate) ÷ (1 − deduction-relief rate). The common growth factor and starting budget cancel.

The matrix displays that ratio minus one as a percentage difference. A positive cell means the modeled RRSP amount is larger; a negative cell means it is smaller. These are amounts relative to the TFSA outcome, not annualized investment returns. Changing the horizon or common investment return does not change this isolated ratio.

The waterfall reconciles the gross RRSP balance, tax at withdrawal and TFSA comparison amount. Tax relief has already financed the gross contribution at the start. Adding the refund to the ending balance again would count the same resource twice.

05

Add the rules and cash-flow constraints before deciding

Actual account choice also depends on available contribution and deduction room, the use date, access needs, withdrawal rules, employer arrangements and the household’s wider tax situation. Check current CRA guidance for those questions rather than extending this simplified illustration beyond its assumptions.

The tool assumes a single deposit and no additional tax drag inside either qualifying account. It omits fees, withholding mechanics, income-tested benefits, future account conversion rules, estate treatment and changes in tax law. A deduction that cannot be fully used now also breaks the immediate-relief assumption.

Document the net saving cost, how the tax relief will be funded and used, and a plausible range for future withdrawal tax. Then compare the result with the goal’s timing and liquidity requirements. A transparent comparison helps identify the variables that need review; the largest gross balance alone does not settle the account decision.
